The Fourcast

What next for Christa Pike as death row inmate WAKES UP after two lethal injections
The unprecedented survival of Christa Pike following a botched lethal injection in Tennessee has plunged the American capital punishment system into a deep legal and constitutional crisis.
Sentenced to death at age 18 for the 1995 murder of Colleen Slemmer, Pike was scheduled to become the first woman executed by the state in over two centuries. However, after two lethal doses of pentobarbital failed to kill her, she survived and was rushed to intensive care.
Pike is now reportedly conscious and speaking in hospital while handcuffed to her bed.
In this episode of The Fourcast, Anushka Asthana is joined by Dr. Joel Zivot, an anaesthesiologist advising Pike's defence team, Robin Maher from the Death Penalty Information Center, and "Surviving Execution" author Ian Woods. The panel asks: Can an execution ever truly be humane, or has America reached a breaking point with capital punishment?
SPECIAL RELATIONSHIP? What the RAF Fairford saga tells us about UK-US relations
The sudden withdrawal of American heavy bombers from RAF Fairford back to the United States follows a major incident near the Gloucestershire airbase. Five men were arrested near the base, with the UK government saying it showed "strong indications" of state-sponsored involvement from Tehran.
So why has the US pulled its bombers from the UK? Has the abrupt departure handed Tehran a tactical and propaganda victory? And what does the saga say about the UK’s special relationship with the US?
On this episode of the Fourcast, Krishnan Guru-Murthy is joined by Dr David Jordan from the Freeman Air and Space Institute, former senior official at the Pentagon, Jim Townsend, as well as Trita Parsi from the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft.
Israel-bound FlyDubai flight CHAOS: what happened? | The Fourcast Indicators
An Israel-bound Flydubai flight plunged more than 14,000 feet in just 30 seconds after the co-pilot allegedly attacked the pilot and tried to take control of the aircraft.
The plane eventually landed safely in Saudi Arabia after passengers and off-duty pilots intervened, but the incident has raised urgent questions about aviation security, insider threats and whether flights to Israel now face a new kind of risk.
Matt Frei and Mark Urban examine what we know so far, why Benjamin Netanyahu has compared the incident to a potential “9/11-style” attack, and what it could mean for Israel, Flydubai and airline security around the world.
There is currently no evidence linking the alleged attack to Iran or a wider terrorist plot.
Does Man City’s golden era now deserve to be FORGOTTEN?
In a seismic ruling that has sent shockwaves through football, Manchester City have been found guilty of dozens of financial charges spanning a nine-year period from 2009 to 2018. The club were found to have systematically misstated financial accounts, arranged disguised funding through "sham" sponsorship agreements, and failed to cooperate in good faith with the league's four-year investigation.
While Manchester City have denied the findings and said they plan to appeal the findings, what punishment could they face - a points deduction? Relegation?
In this episode of The Fourcast, Jordan Jarrett-Bryan is joined by chief football writer Darren Lewis and football finance expert Kieran Maguire, the panel interrogates how badly the Premier League’s brand has been tarnished, what punishments the club could face, and whether the integrity of the modern game can survive.
What would it take to GROW THE ECONOMY? Mariana Mazzucato and Fraser Nelson
Can John Healey deliver the growth Britain desperately needs? At Labour’s conference in Liverpool, the Chancellor promised a new age of industrialisation, more opportunities for young people and an era of political hope. But with the government under pressure to control spending, what does that mean for welfare, public investment and the economy?
In this episode of The Fourcast, Krishnan Guru-Murthy speaks to economist Mariana Mazzucato and Times columnist Fraser Nelson. They debate how Britain can grow its economy, whether welfare reform can get more people into work, and whether the government should cut taxes and regulation or invest more heavily in public services and infrastructure.
Is the horn of AFRICA about to EXPLODE?
Hundreds of thousands of people were killed in a two-year between Tigrayan forces and Ethiopia's government which ended in a peace deal in 2022.
Today the trauma and fear of war creeps back in as both sides accuse each other of launching new offensives.
Earlier this week the TPLF announced a new coalition alongside other militias - some of whom had previously been bitter opponents.
The so-called Alliance for survival is made up of seven armed rebel groups which have been waging their own battles against the Ethiopian government in different parts of the country.
Tigrayan forces have seized three airports in Tigray, and in response Ethiopian airlines have suspended all flights to the region.
But why are things escalating now? Is the clock ticking for the Ethiopian government? And will Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed achieve his goal of accessing the Red Sea?
To understand things better and break it all down we’re joined by Tsedale Lemma, an Ethiopian journalist and founder of the Addis Standard and Nicholas Westcott, former director of the Royal African Society.
Donald Trump meets Xi Jinping - new balance of POWER?
US presidents typically welcome foreign leaders at the White House, but on Wednesday Donald Trump laid out the red carpet to greet China’s premier Xi Jinping.In today’s episode of The Fourcast Indicators, Matt Frei and Mark Urban discuss the future being shaped by the two superpowers, what that means for geopolitics and for the economy. Joining us shortly is Bronwen Maddox, CEO of Chatham House, who has written and spoken extensively about China’s attempt to rule a post-American world, and a book called In Defence of America, on how the US has been taken for granted by the rest of the world.
Could our OBSESSION with free speech threaten DEMOCRACY?
Addressing the UN General Assembly in New York, Prime Minister Andy Burnham warned of an "insidious campaign" of hostile foreign interference aimed at stoking domestic division and eroding democratic trust.
To combat the threat, Burnham announced the creation of the National Centre for Information Defence.
In this episode of The Fourcast, Krishnan Guru-Murthy is joined by disinformation expert and author Nina Jankowicz, the Chair of the Intelligence and Security Committee of Parliament, Lord Beamish, as well as the Conservative MP Alicia Kearns.
They discuss the threat posed by Russia to the UK, the role of tech platforms and whether the new unit could risk the censoring of free speech.
Britain is ‘SKATING ON THIN FISCAL ICE’ - former Bank of England economist 
Can Andy Burnham turn the UK economy around?
With just a few weeks to go until his first Budget, the new prime minister is facing a difficult economic outlook, as he deals with sluggish growth, the rising cost of living and a war in Iran which threatens to send inflation soaring.
In this episode of The Fourcast, Krishnan Guru-Murthy speaks to the former chief economist of the Bank of England Andy Haldane and Channel 4’s Economics Editor Helia Ebrahimi.
They discuss cuts to welfare, the pensions triple lock and Britain’s problem with young NEETS: those not in education, employment or training.
Can Trump block Canada's Europe alliance? 
The EU President Ursula Von der Leyen has offered Canada ‘associate membership of the EU’, a move which Donald Trump called ‘laughable’ - but still threatened ‘serious sanctions’ as punishment.
In this episode of the Fourcast, we ask what Canada’s closer ties with the EU could mean - from tighter trade and defence to what Mark Carney calls 'a beacon for other democracies.' But with the far right rising in Europe, is the Canadian Prime Minister trying to join a club that could soon fall apart?
Leslie Vinjamuri, the President and CEO of the Chicago Council on Global Affairs says Carney is playing a long-game when it comes to the US, picking up support on both sides of the border by standing up to Trump, and that his decision to move closer to the EU is a ‘declaration of independence from King Trump’. While Dr. Linn Selle, head of the Europe division of the German Council on Foreign Relations, argues that the EU is chasing Carney’s star power to help revive its appeal.
Paloma Faith: Ed Sheeran should QUIT TOUR as well over Palestine row
Ed Sheeran has found himself embroiled in a huge row after the rapper Macklemore was dropped as a support act from his tour, after he made comments in support of Palestine.
The Suffolk singer has said he is "not complicit" and that the decision to drop Macklemore was not his. Since then, all the other support acts have pulled out of the tour in support of the rapper.
On this episode of The Fourcast, Krishnan Guru-Murthy speaks with singer Paloma Faith who has publicly supported Macklemore, calling him ‘my hero’ on social media.
They discuss the pressure put on if musicians by business interests, whether music can ever stay out of politics and if musicians can ever truly sit on the fence when it comes to the Israel-Palestine conflict.
Mehdi Hasan: Criticise Israel - not Judaism 
Is British politics becoming more like America, dominated by billionaires, huge donations and increasingly polarised media?
Krishnan Guru-Murthy is joined by journalist and broadcaster Mehdi Hasan, who has returned to the UK to launch Zeteo UK.
They discuss Reform UK’s £72 million in donations from two crypto billionaires, what wealthy political donors might expect in return, Britain’s changing relationship with Israel, Donald Trump and the threat to journalism in America - and whether independent media can rebuild the trust lost by traditional news organisations.
Hasan also discusses the war in Gaza, which he describes as a 'genocide' - Israel strongly rejects allegations of genocide and denies committing war crimes, saying its military operations are conducted in accordance with international law.
What America got WRONG after 9/11 - former US diplomat 
Twenty-five years after 9/11, its consequences are still shaping the world. From Tony Blair and George W Bush to Trump, MAGA and the rise of populism in Europe, how much of today’s politics can be traced back to September 11th?
In today’s episode of The Fourcast Indicators, Matt Frei and Mark Urban look back at the attack that transformed American foreign policy, ushered in the war on terror and dramatically expanded the power of intelligence agencies and surveillance.
They are joined by Ambassador Nicholas Burns, the US ambassador to NATO on 9/11, who reveals how America’s allies responded in the hours after the attack, why he now regrets supporting the invasion of Iraq, and what the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan did to America’s willingness to intervene overseas.
Could Britain’s Israel sanctions actually HELP Netanyahu?
The UK has signalled a major change in its approach to Israel, after its Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband announced what he called a “reset” of relations, as well banning exports from illegal Israeli settlements.
And while the move has been praised by many, it has attracted condemnation from Washington and Israel, who in response announced they would close the British consulate in Jerusalem.
So is the move mainly a symbolic gesture from the British government? Or could it signify a major policy shift when it comes to its once close ally?
On this episode of the Fourcast, Matt Frei is joined by the Palestinian Ambassador to the UK, Husam Zomlot, the Labour Chair of the Foreign Affairs Select Committee Dame Emily Thornberry MP, as well as former Conservative Foreign Secretary Sir Malcolm Rifkind.
The far-right WIN BIG in Germany - what comes next?
Germany’s far-right party has won a major victory in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, although it remains to be seen whether the AfD will be able to form a government there.
Nevertheless, the result has sent shockwaves not only through Germany, but across Europe too. For the first time since the end of the Second World War, a far-right party could gain power in a German state.
Why is the AfD surging? How much is its success being driven by immigration, economic frustration and anger at the political establishment? And what could its rise mean for Germany’s relationship with Russia, NATO and the EU?
Matt Frei is joined by author and commentator John Kampfner and Dr Sarah Wagner, a researcher in political science at Queen’s University Belfast, to examine whether this is a political blip or a watershed moment for Germany and Europe.
Reform CAUGHT ON CAMERA - The foreign money scandal
Senior Reform officials have been caught on camera discussing ways to get thousands of pounds of foreign money into the party, potentially breaking electoral law.[Subscribe to our Substack newsletter: https://channel4news.substack.com/subscribe]A Channel 4 News and Verbatim Investigations investigation found that James Orr, Reform’s Head of Policy, and Dan Jukes, a close aide to Nigel Farage, arranged for a US company to secretly fund three influential polls commissioned by the party. Since we aired the story, the two officials involved have stepped down from their positions but deny wrongdoing, and rival parties have reported Reform to the police. The Reform party has denied wrongdoing and launched an internal investigation. Nigel Farage has insisted that the party has broken no laws.To discuss all of this, Krishnan Guru-Murthy is joined by political commentator and former Reform member Tim Montgomerie, Labour MP Dame Emily Thornberry, as well as the barrister and election law expert Tom Gillie.
A ‘SUPERSIZED’ El Niño is coming. Can we handle the economic shock? 
A potentially “supersized” El Niño is forecast for this winter - and scientists warn it could bring more extreme weather, from droughts and heatwaves to devastating floods.
But what happens when El Niño collides with a world already being reshaped by climate change?
On this episode of The Fourcast, Krishnan Guru-Murthy asks whether governments, businesses and the global financial system are prepared for the shocks ahead.
He speaks to Liz Stephens, Professor of Climate Risks and Resilience at the University of Reading and an anticipatory action expert at the Red Cross Red Crescent Climate Centre, who explains how early warning systems can help communities prepare before disaster strikes, and economist Dr Matthew Winning, from UCL’s Institute for Sustainable Resources, looks at the wider economic consequences - from food prices and supply chains to insurance, investment and our pensions.
As extreme weather becomes harder to predict, should we rethink the way we plan for disasters? And is it already too late to rely on the old idea of a “one-in-100-year” event?
‘A BATTLE FOR SURVIVAL’ - Iran plunged back into war 
Hopes for a diplomatic breakthrough have faded as retaliatory strikes flare up once again across the Middle East. And with Donald Trump warning of further military escalation, is the world at risk of yet another economic shock?
So what’s behind the new wave of strikes in the Middle East? And could Iran be at risk of losing control of its ultimate bargaining chip - the Strait of Hormuz.
In this episode of The Fourcast Indicators, Krishnan Guru-Murthy and Mark Urban break down the geopolitical signals shaping this war. Joined by the economist Neil Shearing from Capital Economics, they discuss global markets, inflation, and whether an exit strategy exists for either side.
‘TRUMP’S A CATASTROPHE FOR THE WORLD’ - Mohammed Marandi on 6 months of war
Pakistan is the latest country to hit back after the White House threatened countries who trade with Iran. China has already said it won’t be taking orders from America. So is this another failed bid by Donald Trump to bend Iran and its backers to his will?
Or could this actually work? Several senior Iranian leaders have recently acknowledged the economic pain that the country and its people are feeling.
On this episode of The Fourcast, Krishnan Guru-Murthy speaks to Mohammed Marandi, a professor at Tehran University and a former adviser to Iran’s nuclear negotiating team to get a view from inside Iran.
END OF SOCIAL MEDIA? What Meta’s landmark case means for future of social media 
Meta has agreed to a landmark settlement over allegations that its platforms harmed children and teenagers - raising a much bigger question about how social media is designed and regulated.
On this episode of The Fourcast, we look at what the settlement actually means for Instagram and Facebook users, whether other social media companies could be forced to follow suit, and whether this could fundamentally change the way we use social media.
Krishnan Guru-Murthy was joined by visiting professor at Stony Brook University School of Journalism and author of ‘Hot Type’ Jeff Jarvis and Associate Professor in Digital Humanities at University College London, Kaitlyn Regehr.
In a statement released after the settlement, Meta said the agreement is not an admission of wrongdoing, but a new framework designed to give parents more control and teenagers stronger protections. It says the measures will only work if TikTok and YouTube adopt the same rules, because teenagers move between multiple platforms.
‘America is now a friend of Russia’ - has Trump HELPED PUTIN?
Britain is doubling down on its support for Ukraine, backing a deal that could see Ukraine produce its own long-range missiles as Russia intensifies its attacks.
But as Moscow ramps up its missile production and warns of further mobilisation, Ukraine is facing growing pressure on its air defences and ammunition supplies. Meanwhile, questions remain over whether Europe can fill the gap if US support continues to weaken.
On this episode of The Fourcast, Krishnan Guru Murthy is joined by Channel 4 News International Editor Lindsey Hilsum and Guardian foreign correspondent Luke Harding to discuss Britain's growing role in the war, the state of the battlefield and whether Ukraine's allies are becoming weary of the conflict.
Could long-range Ukrainian missiles change the war? Is Russia winning the war of attrition? And how far is Britain prepared to go to support Ukraine?
$40 TRILLION 'TIME BOMB': Is Trump about to break the global economy? 
Is Donald Trump driving the world economy off a cliff while you’re on your summer holiday?
America has just passed $40 trillion of debt. Trump’s tariffs are pushing up prices, his tax cuts are adding to the deficit, and his war with Iran has sent oil prices soaring.
Now bond markets are turning on him. The US treasury has tried to step in and calm the bond markets, but it doesn’t appear to have worked.
So what exactly is going on? Is this just a wobble in the bond markets - or a sign of something much worse to come?
On this episode of The Fourcast, Ciaran Jenkins is joined by Pippa Malmgren, who served as an economic adviser to President Bush, and The Economist’s Archie Hall.
Is it time for BILLIONAIRES to PAY UP? Wealth tax debate
Should Britain tax wealth more heavily? With the government under pressure to find billions for public services and defence, Andy Burnham has refused to rule out a wealth tax.
But would taxing the richest households actually raise significant money, or drive wealth, investment and entrepreneurs out of the country?
On The Fourcast, Matt Frei is joined by Gabriel Zucman, economist and author of 'We Need to Tax Billionaires' and economist Arthur Laffer, creator of the Laffer Curve.
So how unequal is Britain? Has wealth become undertaxed compared with income? And if Britain doesn't tax the richest more, where else should the government find the money?
The HUMILIATION that Farage might NEVER recover from
Nigel Farage has secured re-election in the Clacton by-election, but his political gamble to "stick two fingers up to the establishment" hasn’t gone according to plan. With novelty candidate Count Binface as Farage’s primary challenger, the self-described intergalactic space warrior secured nearly 10,000 votes.
With Farage's personal favorability ratings dropping and accusations that he skipped the declaration to avoid being "humiliated by nobodies," has the Reform leader’s publicity stunt severely backfired?
In this episode of The Fourcast, Alex Thomson speaks to Popular Conservatism director Mark Littlewood, columnist Sonia Sodha, and polling expert Luke Tryl (Reform UK were unable to find anyone from the party to appear on the podcast).
They analyse whether Reform UK is losing its political momentum, how the ongoing standards investigation affects Farage's future, and whether Britain's political right is facing a deep crisis of credibility.
‘THIS IS A LAND GRAB’ - Israeli settler West Bank siege explained
In the West Bank village of Qusra, Israeli settlers have spent days besieging Palestinian homes, cutting residents off from food and water - an attack even Donald Trump’s ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, has condemned as a “horrific act of terror”.
But this incident appears to be part of an escalation of settler violence in the West Bank this year.
So can Benjamin Netanyahu and his government, who have at times condemned the violence but have also done so much to embolden settlers, reign it in? Or is the situation spiralling out of control?
In a statement, the Israeli military said that soldiers had been deployed in Qusra since Thursday morning to protect residents and maintain security, and "were instructed that the Qusra residents will remain in their homes."
The military added that "soldiers will not operate inside the Palestinian family's home located near the site where the tent that was evacuated and dismantled had been erected".
On this episode of The Fourcast, Matt Frei is joined by former Israeli ambassador to Canada Alan Baker, who was part of a commission set up by Benjamin Netanyahu to investigate the legality of settlements in the West Bank. He was also joined by Palestinian ambassador to Unesco Adel Atieh and Haaretz senior analyst Esther Solomon.
The Tories gave us NET ZERO - why have they given up on it?
In 2019, Theresa May positioned the UK as a global climate leader by enshrining a legally binding Net Zero target by 2050. Fast forward seven years, and the political landscape on the British Right has transformed dramatically. With Conservative Leader Kemi Badenoch proposing to repeal Net Zero targets and Reform UK labeling green policies "net-stupid-zero," the consensus around climate action is fracturing.
All this comes as the UK endures repeated heatwaves, droughts, and severe economic impacts—with summer heatwaves costing an estimated £4.4bn in lost productivity alongside thousands of excess deaths. As extreme weather directly threatens agriculture and rural communities, is the Right out of step with voters, or are they tapping into growing cost-of-living concerns?
In this episode of The Fourcast, Matt Frei explores whether Net Zero scepticism is pragmatic economics or climate denial in disguise. Matt is joined by former Energy Minister Graham Stuart MP, Net Zero Scrutiny Group member Lord Peter Lilley, and former NFU President Baroness Minette Batters to debate conservative ideology, economic reality, and the electoral risks facing the Right.
Have AIs GONE ROGUE? These cyber experts told us what's behind the recent hackings
AI is increasingly being used to find vulnerabilities, exploit networks and carry out cyberattacks - but how autonomous are these systems really?
On this episode of The Fourcast, Matt Frei asks whether we are approaching a world where AI agents can conduct cyberattacks with little or no human intervention. Could an AI maintain access to a network, evade attempts to shut it down or even copy itself?
Matt is joined by AI safety expert and author of Considerations on the AI Endgame, Dr Roman V. Yampolskiy, and Katie Moussouris, founder and CEO of Luta Security and a former contributor to the US government's ‘Hack the Pentagon’ programme.
They discuss the latest AI hacking incidents, whether governments need tougher regulation, who should be responsible when AI causes harm, and whether AI could ultimately become both the biggest cyber threat - and the best defence against it.
‘PUTIN’S NIGHTMARE’: how Ukraine can deliver ‘KILLER BLOW’ in Russia war | The Fourcast: Indicators
The war in Ukraine appears to have entered a new phase, as Kyiv has launched increasingly ambitious long-range strikes deep inside Russia, put mounting pressure on Crimea and sought to bring the war closer to ordinary Russians and Vladimir Putin.
But now the Kremlin is hitting back hard. In a missile attack on Kyiv this week, at least 17 people were killed. Now there’s reports of a Ukrainian plane in Leipzig, Germany, being targeted by an explosive-laden drone. It’s not clear who was behind the attack but reporting suggests it could be Russia. So are we witnessing a dangerous new phase of escalation?
On this episode of the Fourcast Indicators, Matt Frei and Mark Urban are joined by economist Timothy Ash from Chatham House’s Russia and Eurasia programme.
Farage’s ratings PLUMMET: What’s going on with Reform?
Just a few months ago, Nigel Farage and Reform UK looked unstoppable. After sweeping the local elections and topping opinion polls, many believed Reform was on course for government. But has the momentum already begun to fade?
A string of controversies - including police investigations, questions over party finances, and a £5 million donation from a Thailand-based cryptocurrency billionaire - has put Reform under growing pressure. With the party slipping in the polls, are these scandals finally cutting through with voters, or is this just another setback Farage will survive?
On this episode of The Fourcast, Matt Frei is joined by Tim Ross from Politico, former Reform UK spokesperson Gawain Towler and Labour strategist Claire Ainsley to examine what's gone wrong for Reform, whether Andy Burnham has given Labour a route back to power, why the Greens are also losing ground, and what the latest polling tells us about the future of British politics.
Moroccan Migrant incident: Why the right say UK could be invaded 
After around 50,000 migrants crossed into Spain’s North African territory of Ceuta, far-right politicians across Europe quickly branded the events an "invasion." But with most migrants already returning to Morocco and UK illegal boat crossings dropping to a five-year low—down 43% compared to 2025—what is actually driving the debate around European border control?
On this episode of The Fourcast, Matt Frei is joined by Director of the Migration Observatory Madeleine Sumption, Director of Politics at Ipsos Keiran Pedley, and Austrian migration expert Gerald Knaus.
They discuss whether the incident in Ceuta could drive a new surge for the far-right across Europe, how the UK could be affected and if immigration is still the hot topic for voters.
Will Gianni Infantino RESIGN over his botched World Cup deal?
Despite his job seemingly looking assured just a few weeks ago, Gianni Infantino’s position as President of FIFA is now in jeopardy.
With the footballing federations of Europe, North America and Asia all rejecting Infantino’s plans to sell off part of the World Cup to private investors, pressure is piling on Infantino. Even the new Prime Minister Andy Burnham says Infantino is the “wrong man” to lead FIFA.
On this episode of The Fourcast, Matt Frei is joined by Channel 4’s Sports Reporter, Jordan Jarrett-Bryan, as well as Abiola Ijasanmi the former Chief Operating Officer from the Confederation of African Football.
They discuss whether Infantino has badly mis-read the situation and - could he actually could be forced out of this job?
 The ROAD TO WWIII? The Iran war escalates | The Fourcast Indicators
The war between the United States and Iran has spread across the Middle East.
Fresh strikes in Saudi Arabia, Iraq and Egypt, alongside escalating Houthi attacks on international shipping, have raised fears that the region is entering a dangerous new phase. With Washington intensifying its military campaign and Iran relying on its network of allied militias, is this becoming a wider regional war?
On this episode of The Fourcast: Indicators, Matt Frei and Mark Urban are joined by Professor Madawi al-Rasheed from the London School of Economics Middle East Centre. They discuss why the Houthis are stepping up attacks, whether Saudi Arabia is being pulled into the fighting despite its efforts to avoid it, how Iraqi militias could become a new flashpoint, and whether the US has a long-term strategy, or is being drawn into another prolonged Middle East war.
Is there still a path to de-escalation, or are we witnessing the beginning of a conflict that could engulf the wider region?
Why has EVERYONE FAILED to fix social care?
Social care is the thorny issue which politicians have failed to solve for decades.
Today though, the new Prime Minister Andy Burnham put it back on the political agenda as he called for a ‘National Care Service’, saying that social care in the UK is “as unfair” as the healthcare system in the US.
On this week’s episode of The Fourcast, Matt Frei is joined by the former Conservative Work and Pensions Secretary Damien Green, Professor Richard Humphries who is a Senior Policy Advisor at the Health Foundation and the Liberal Democrat MP and Chair of the Health Select Committee Layla Moran.
They discuss why the current system is not fit for purpose, why previous efforts at reform have failed and whether Andy Burnham could be the one to finally solve it.
European wildfires RAGE: Are politicians fanning the flames?
As thousands of people are forced to flee their homes amid devastating wildfires in France, Spain and Scotland, the climate emergency seems closer to people’s lives than ever.
Despite this, governments around the world are seemingly rolling back their efforts to end the fossil fuel pollution that is driving the climate emergency.
On this episode of The Fourcast, Matt Frei is joined by environmentalist George Monbiot, Professor Liz Bentley from the Royal Meteorological Society and Fiona Macklin, Head of Climate at Apolitical.
They discuss what it will take to finally get politicians to start taking global heating seriously. And whether even when disaster is staring us in the face, if we as a people are really ready to make the changes necessary?
ZOMBIE TARIFFS: Why Trump’s favourite idea won’t go away
Months after many of his ‘Liberation Day’ tariffs were declared illegal by the Supreme Court, Donald Trump has announced a fresh wave of tariffs against dozens of countries.
This time, using the allegation of “forced labour” by America’s trading partners, Trump is hoping his new tariffs will be less open to challenge in the courts.
But what will the impact be on American consumers already hit hard by the war in Iran? And can anyone take Trump’s trade policy seriously, when it can all change in an instant?
On this episode of The Fourcast, Matt Frei is joined by Australian-American economist Justin Wolfers, as well as Financial Times columnist and co-author of the book How to Win a Trade War, Soumaya Keynes.
Could Trump deal lead to Saudi NUKES?
The US and Saudi Arabia have reportedly signed a landmark deal that could pave the way for a Saudi nuclear programme, sparking fears it could eventually allow the Gulf kingdom to develop its own nuclear weapon.
President Donald Trump has denied that the agreement permits Saudi Arabia to enrich uranium, and says any deal is dependent on Riyadh joining the Abraham Accords and recognising Israel, a move many experts say remains unlikely.
Meanwhile, tensions in the region have escalated after Houthi attacks on Saudi ships in the Bab el Mandab strait pushed oil prices higher. Trump has warned that further attacks could trigger “major military punishment” against Iran and the Houthis.
On this episode of The Fourcast, Matt Frei is joined by Channel 4 News foreign affairs correspondent Jonathan Rugman to examine the US-Saudi nuclear deal, the growing confrontation with the Houthis, and what it means for the future of the Middle East.
Zelenskyy SACKS top general - is this Ukraine's BIGGEST WARTIME CRISIS? | The Fourcast Indicators
Why has Volodymyr Zelenskyy reshuffled Ukraine's military leadership at a crucial moment in the war against Russia?
As Kyiv ramps up its long-range drone campaign deep inside Russia, Ukraine's president has appointed General Mykhailo Drapatyi to lead the country's armed forces. Supporters say he's the innovative commander Ukraine needs for the next phase of the conflict—but why make such a significant change when the war appears to be swinging in Ukraine's favour?
On this episode of The Fourcast: Indicators, Matt Frei and Mark Urban examine what Zelenskyy's military shake-up signals, whether Ukraine is rewriting the rules of modern warfare, and if drones can continue to shift the balance against Russia. They're joined by Orysia Lutsevych, Head of the Ukraine Forum at Chatham House, to discuss the challenges facing Kyiv, what Vladimir Putin may do next, and the wider security picture, including Houthi attacks in the Red Sea and the emerging US-Saudi nuclear agreement.
How RADICAL will Andy Burnham be on the economy? 
Andy Burnham is Britain's new prime minister.
On his first day in Downing Street, he promised the biggest changes to Britain in 40 years, unveiled his vision for government and began assembling his cabinet. But what do those first decisions tell us about the kind of Prime Minister he wants to be?
In this episode of The Fourcast, Anushka Asthana examines Burnham's first speech and the challenges waiting in his in-tray. Can he rebuild trust in politics? How different is ‘Burnhamism’ from the Starmer years? And with Britain's public finances under huge pressure, can he improve living standards without returning to austerity or breaking Labour's tax promises?
Joining Anushka today are Neal Lawson, a close ally of Burnham’s who co-founded the influential left wing group Compass, political strategist Peter Hyman, who was at the heart of the Downing Street operation in the Blair years and a senior adviser to Keir Starmer in opposition, and Political Editor at the i Paper, Caroline Wheeler.
Trump-Infantino: is this the World Cup that BROKE FIFA?
The World Cup final is here. But could this tournament be remembered more for its politics than its football - from Donald Trump's travel restrictions, to soaring ticket prices and growing criticism of FIFA's relationship with the White House, controversy has followed this World Cup from the very beginning.
At the centre of it all is FIFA president Gianni Infantino. Once elected promising to clean up football's governing body after the Sepp Blatter era, he's now facing mounting criticism from across the game. So, has Infantino gone too far? Could his grip on FIFA finally be weakening? Or is he more powerful than ever?
On this episode of The Fourcast, Jordan Jarrett-Bryan is joined by broadcaster and football journalist Kate Mason and Carl Anka from the Athletic.
Iran war oil shock: world economy on brink of something ‘EVEN WORSE’
President Donald Trump has U-turned on his threat to charge cargo ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz as much as 20% - but the US and Iran have continued trading strikes as Trump has told the US Congress that war has resumed.
So, can the US gain the upper hand? Will more US bombs and bullets really help? And has this whole episode proven that the memorandum of understanding, which was meant to end the conflict, was destined to fail.

sources.text:
Christa Pike, the Tennessee inmate who survived a botched execution attempt last week, is awake and speaking, her attorneys said Tuesday.
“Against all odds, Christa Pike is conscious, speaking, and continues to receive critical medical care,” Pike’s attorneys said in a statement to HuffPost. “Despite the severe damage she endured to her arms, she is still handcuffed and shackled to the bed. Her recovery is medically unprecedented. Her prognosis remains unclear but, at a minimum, we expect a long recovery.”
Pike, 50, became one of the youngest women sent to death row when she and her boyfriend tortured and killed classmate Colleen Slemmer in 1995, when Pike was 18.
Last Wednesday, on the night of her execution, Pike was given two doses of the lethal injection drug pentobarbital. The pentobarbital didn’t kill her, but instead left her critically injured. Pike was hospitalized, unconscious and also placed on a ventilator for several days.
In their statement, Pike’s attorneys called on Tennessee Republican Gov. Bill Lee to commute her sentence.
“Christa is a survivor and will take recovery one day at a time,” the statement said. “We continue to ask the Governor of Tennessee to commute Christa Pike’s sentence to life imprisonment without the possibility of parole.” Pike’s attorneys will be in court Wednesday to seek more information about the failed execution attempt, and said they will hold a press conference following the hearing.

sources.news_title: Christa Pike is angry and confused after surviving execution attempt, attorney says
sources.text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (AP) — Christa Pike was “angry and confused” in the hours after regaining consciousness following Tennessee’s failed execution attempt, first asking, “Where am I?” her lawyer said Wednesday.
Pike, believed to be the first person to survive after receiving lethal injection drugs during an execution, stunningly woke up as plans were being made to remove her from life support, just six days after she was strapped to a gurney in the death chamber, said attorney Randy Spivey.
“But on Tuesday, to the shock of everyone ... Christa woke up and began talking,” Spivey said.
Pike, who was sentenced to death for the 1995 beating and stabbing death of classmate Colleen Slemmer, is aware of what happened to her, at least up to a point, Spivey said.
Many questions remain, though, about her prognosis for recovery and whether Tennessee will make another attempt to execute Pike, now age 50.
Her lawyers said Wednesday that she has suffered enough and want the governor to commute her sentence. A judge in Nashville told the state on Wednesday to save evidence from the execution attempt as Pike's attorneys try to find out more.
The failed execution on Sept. 30 has renewed scrutiny of how states carry out the death penalty, in particular the use of lethal injection. Texas was set to carry out Wednesday the first execution in the U.S. since Tennessee attempted to put Pike to death.
Pike faces a long recovery, lawyer says
Pike's legal team said she still can’t move her arms or swallow and has some cognitive confusion. She also has pneumonia and a blood clot in her arm, Spivey said. Her hands were extremely swollen when they saw her Tuesday in the hospital, shackled to a bed, he added.
Her prognosis remains unclear and she has a long road to recovery, he said.
“She is angry and confused about everything right now,” Randy Spivey said during a news conference following a court hearing about preserving evidence.
Spivey, who was not with Pike when she woke up, was told her first words were, “Where am I?” and “Who are you?”
Pike’s attorneys want evidence preserved
The Death Penalty Information Center says Pike is the first person to survive after receiving lethal injection drugs during an execution.
At the hearing Wednesday, a judge told the state that the Tennessee Department of Correction needs to save evidence including “anything that was in the actual room.”
Chancery Court Judge I’Ashea Myles said she plans to issue a sweeping order that will direct the state to maintain recordings, witness accounts, emails, drugs, syringes, IV lines and other medical items.
The Tennessee Attorney General's Office had argued a court order was unnecessary. John W. Ayers, assistant attorney general, said some evidence from the death chamber already had been collected and logged. He declined to comment after the hearing.
Pike's attorneys accused the state of carrying out the attempted execution in secrecy, saying more transparency is needed. They also repeated their calls for clemency for Pike. Republican Gov. Bill Lee has not yet indicated how he'll respond.
Outside the courthouse, Michelle Nowell yelled “Justice for Colleen” as Pike's attorneys talked with supporters.
“The victim is Colleen. The victim is not Christa Pike,” said Nowell, who was among a group outside the prison last week where the failed execution took place.
What happened in the execution chamber remains unclear
The governor postponed the state’s only other execution for this year and ordered a review of what went wrong. The state’s prison chief resigned.
Medical and lethal injection experts have focused on the possibility that a problem with the IV line caused the drug to pool in her tissue rather than entering her bloodstream.
Pike’s attorneys wrote in a court filing that “apparently at no point did any member of the execution team realize that the IV lines were not correctly placed or that the veins had blown.”
State officials have not yet offered an explanation.
The attempted execution got underway when Pike was given a chance to make a final statement. About five minutes later, she raised her head and said her arm was hurting. At some point she appeared to lose consciousness, but she could be heard breathing heavily until media were escorted from the witness room nearly 90 minutes into the execution. An ambulance took Pike to a hospital.
Dr. Joel Zivot, a professor of anesthesiology and surgery in Atlanta who consulted as an expert for Pike’s legal team, said it could be weeks or months before anyone knows exactly what her recovery might look like, and whether her competency could be restored so the state can try again to execute her.
Associated Press writers Ed White in Detroit and John Seewer, in Toledo, Ohio, contributed.

Christa Pike, a 50-year-old convicted of a 1995 murder, survived an execution attempt in Tennessee that authorities have acknowledged did not proceed as planned. Medical experts advising her defense suggested the drug did not adequately enter her bloodstream, instead accumulating in tissue beneath her skin.
Pike’s legal representatives had previously raised concerns about her medical condition of thrombocytosis, a blood-clotting disorder that could potentially interfere with intravenous administration. Her full long-term medical condition remains unclear. The state’s Department of Correction Commissioner has announced plans to step down.

Legal experts note that the U.S. Supreme Court has historically permitted second execution attempts after failed procedures. Pike is believed to be the only individual to survive after receiving a lethal injection, distinguishing her case from seven other documented instances of execution survivors who were never successfully injected with lethal drugs.

sources.news_title: Hearing set on motion to preserve evidence in Christa Pike’s botched execution
sources.text:
A hearing is set for Wednesday on a motion to preserve evidence in the botched execution of Christa Pike.
The lone woman on Tennessee’s death row survived being administered two lethal doses of pentobarbital and remains hospitalized following the failed Sept. 30 execution in Nashville, her attorneys said.
Pike was sentenced to death after being convicted of the 1995 murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer. Her attempted execution by lethal injection came after a series of last-minute legal challenges.
Pike’s attorneys filed an emergency motion in Davidson County Chancery Court last week seeking an order requiring the Tennessee Department of Correction to protect and preserve “any and all evidence related” related to the execution attempt, which they allege was “cruel and unusual punishment.”
“In light of the manifest violation of Ms. Pike’s constitutional rights, the actionable nature of that violation, and the reasonable foreseeability of litigation, the Defendants have an affirmative duty to preserve all relevant physical, written, and electronic evidence,” the filing stated.
A status conference on the matter has been scheduled for 11 a.m. CT Wednesday.
According to the motion, Pike “could be heard crying, whimpering, and breathing loudly” while being administered two lethal doses of pentobarbital, at one point stating that her arm “feels like it’s about to burst open.” At least seven needles were used to gain IV access, with one “bent in a 90-degree angle when it was removed,” the motion stated.
The motion described pentobarbital, a sedating medication, as being “caustic and highly alkaline” and that it “burns upon contact.” Both of Pike’s arms were “swollen, burned, and blistered” when she arrived at a Nashville-area hospital, the motion stated.
Pike had raised concerns about a lethal injection in the months prior to her scheduled execution, arguing that her “thrombocytosis, post traumatic stress disorder and small veins ‘make it sure or very likely that there is a substantial risk that she will experience unnecessary and superadded pain and suffering, terror, and disgrace,"” the motion stated.
In an update Tuesday, Pike’s attorneys said she was conscious and speaking after the failed execution left her critically injured and temporarily on a ventilator.
“Her recovery is medically unprecedented. Her prognosis remains unclear but, at a minimum, we expect a long recovery,” her attorneys — Randy Spivey and Kelly Gleason from the Tennessee Office of the Post Conviction Defender and Stephen Ferrell and Luke Ihnen from Federal Defender Services of Eastern Tennessee — said in a statement.
The Tennessee Department of Correction confirmed Tuesday that Pike remains hospitalized but said it could not provide details of her medical condition due to federal privacy laws.
“We can say only that Christa Pike remains hospitalized at the Nashville-area facility where she was transported by emergency services on September 30,” the department said in a statement. “Federal privacy laws prevent TDOC from sharing or confirming her medical information.”
Pike’s attorneys said Tuesday they continue to ask Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee to commute her sentence to life imprisonment without the possibility of parole.
She is the first person reported to have survived lethal injection after being given medications, according to the Death Penalty Information Center, whose executive director referred to the failed attempt as “the worst we’ve ever seen and unlike any other botched execution in the modern era.”
In the wake of the botched execution, Lee ordered a temporary halt to scheduled executions in the state and Tennessee Department of Correction Commissioner Frank Strada resigned.
The governor’s office said in a statement that it has also appointed former U.S. Attorney Ed Stanton to conduct an independent review of the Tennessee Department of Correction’s execution attempt that “will seek to determine whether the protocol was followed and consider whether additional recommendations are necessary to ensure the State’s protocol continues to be lawful and effective.”
“The State previously retained Stanton in 2022 to conduct an independent review of Tennessee’s lethal injection protocol. His work prompted the State and Attorney General’s Office to substantially rewrite the protocol before executions resumed,” the statement further said.

Christa Pike Awake And Speaking In Tennessee Hospital After Failed Execution
Christa Pike, the woman who survived a botched execution last week, is awake and speaking.
NBC News reports that Pike’s attorneys announced on Tuesday that she is currently handcuffed to her hospital bed and suffered significant injuries to her arm as a result of the failed execution. Pike’s execution was called off last week after executioners administered two doses of pentobarbital that failed to kill her. “At a minimum, we expect a long recovery,” attorneys Randy Spivey and Kelly Gleason said. “We are incredibly grateful to the first responders and the medical team at the hospital who treated Christa like a human and have provided exceptional care to her. We also want to thank thousands from all over the world who sent messages offering prayers and support for Christa.”
Pike’s prognosis is still unclear, and her attorneys said her arm was burned and blistered due to the failed execution. According to AP, the Death Penalty Information Center says Pike is the only person to survive after receiving lethal injection drugs during an execution.
Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee canceled all remaining executions for the year and ordered an investigation into what happened. Pike’s attorneys believe that issues with the IV line caused the pentobarbital to spread into her body as opposed to her bloodstream.
CNN reports that former Tennessee prisons chief, Frank Strada, has a history of botched executions. As an official in Arizona’s prison system, Strada raised concerns due to executioners flouting established protocol. This was also the second botched execution in Tennessee this year under Strada’s purview.
In a statement announcing his resignation, Strada said he believed the state Department of Correction had carried out its responsibilities “in accordance with the established protocol,” but his resignation was in the “best interest of Tennesseans as the independent review moves forward.”
The fact that Strada got the job despite having a history of botched executions only drives home the impression that you don’t have to actually be good at your job to be in law enforcement.
Pike’s legal team has called for her sentence to be commuted due to the failed execution. “The least that could happen now is that we at least take death off the table and start looking for what the future could be for her,” attorney Steve Ferrell, of the Federal Defender Services of Eastern Tennessee, told CBS News.
Conversely, May Martinez, Slemmer’s mom, said that the Tennessee authorities need to “make this right” and keep Pike on Death Row. She added that, as a result of the failed execution, state officials, including Lee, “owe me big time.”

“She is angry and confused about everything right now. ... She is very aware of what they did to her up to a point,” he said.
According to Pike’s attorneys, she has a blood clot, cannot swallow and has not eaten. Her arms and hands are swollen and it is unknown at this time if she will regain function in her arms. They also said she has pneumonia.
“The swelling was extraordinary,” Spivey said.
Pike’s feet and right arm are shackled to her hospital bed. Medical staff and her attorneys have asked for some of the restraints to be removed, according to her legal team.

Pike, 50, survived even after executioners tried to give her two lethal doses of pentobarbital on Sept. 30. She was sentenced to death for the 1995 beating and stabbing death of classmate Colleen Slemmer.
The Death Penalty Information Center says Pike is the only person to survive after receiving lethal injection drugs during an execution.
At a hearing Wednesday in Nashville, Pike’s attorneys asked the court to order the Tennessee Department of Correction to save evidence in the case and provide more information about what went wrong. A judge ordered the state to preserve “anything that was in the actual room.”
“Part of the issue that we are facing is that, up until yesterday, our client was unconscious, unable to communicate with counsel, unable to communicate with medical providers, and without her consent, a new lawsuit cannot be filed, Luke Ihnen, a federal public defender, told the court.
Her legal team said Tuesday that Pike’s prognosis remains unclear and, at a minimum, she faces a lengthy recovery. Her arms were burned and blistered after the attempted lethal injection and she is handcuffed to the hospital bed, they said.
The failed execution has renewed scrutiny of how states carry out the death penalty, in particular the use of lethal injection. Texas was set to carry out Wednesday the first execution in the U.S. since Tennessee attempted to put Pike to death.
Christa Pike’s attorneys want evidence preserved
Pike’s attorneys wanted a court order to require the prison system to preserve information from the attempted execution, including drug lot numbers, needles, execution logs and other information.
Chancery Court Judge I’Ashea Myles indicated that her order to save the evidence would be sweeping, saying the state should maintain recordings, witness accounts, emails along with drugs, syringes, IV lines and other medical items.
The Tennessee Attorney General’s Office said a court order was unnecessary. John W. Ayers, assistant attorney general, said evidence from the death chamber already had been collected and logged.
Republican Gov. Bill Lee has called what happened “deeply disturbing” and ordered a “comprehensive, third-party review to determine exactly what occurred.” The governor postponed the state’s only other execution scheduled for this year.
The state’s prison chief resigned in the wake of the failed execution.
Christa Pike’s recovery remains uncertain
Medical and lethal injection experts have focused on the possibility that a problem with the IV line caused the drug to pool in her tissue rather than entering her bloodstream. Pike’s attorneys wrote in their court filing that “apparently at no point did any member of the execution team realize that the IV lines were not correctly placed or that the veins had blown.”
The attempted execution got underway around 7:30 p.m. on Sept. 30 when Pike was given a chance to make a final statement. About five minutes later, Pike raised her head and said her arm was hurting. At some point she appeared to lose consciousness, but she could be heard audibly breathing until media were escorted from the witness room at 8:53 p.m. An ambulance arrived at the prison at 9:14 p.m. to take Pike to a hospital.
Dr. Joel Zivot, a professor of anesthesiology and surgery in Atlanta who consulted as an expert for Pike’s legal team, said it could be weeks or months before anyone knows exactly what her recovery might look like, and whether her competency could be restored so the state can try again to execute her.

US execution survivor Christa Pike is awake and speaking
WASHINGTON — US death row inmate Christa Pike, who survived Tennessee's effort to execute her by lethal injection last week, foiling the state's first attempt to put a woman to death in two centuries, has regained consciousness and is speaking, her lawyers said in a statement on Tuesday.
Pike, 50, continues to receive critical medical care while "handcuffed and shackled to the bed" in hospital, her lawyers said in a statement on Tuesday.
Pike, who was sentenced to death after murdering Colleen Slemmer with her then-boyfriend in 1995, survived two failed lethal injections last Wednesday in Tennessee.
She was taken to hospital, where she remained unconscious for days as medical staff cleared her body of the injected chemical. Experts and her legal team say her apparent recovery is unprecedented.
Pike is believed to be the only person to survive a lethal injection.
"Her prognosis remains unclear, but at a minimum we expect a long recovery," her lawyers said, adding that a court hearing on Pike's case was scheduled for Wednesday in Davidson County Chancery Court.
The hearing pertains to her lawyers' request for a court order to preserve evidence from the failed execution they said would show the Tennessee Department of Correction violated Pike's constitutional rights by subjecting her to cruel and unusual punishment, a spokesperson said.
Deborah Denno, a criminologist and professor at Fordham Law School, said she was "absolutely astonished" that Pike was conscious and speaking.
There had been seven other cases where prisoners survived executions but in those cases, executioners were not able to inject anything into the inmates' veins, Denno said.
Pike "is the only person for whom some kind of toxin has been injected", she said.
"They did everything they were supposed to do as part of the execution process, and it simply didn't work," Denno said. "This has never happened before."
Steven Hale, a journalist for the Nashville Banner, said the case raised many questions, including "what must this be like for the victim's family, who for 30 years has been told we are gonna give you justice and justice is us executing Christa Pike".
Authorities have not yet said whether they will try again to execute Pike. They have also not offered an explanation for what went wrong after twice injecting her with the chemical pentobarbital.
Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has suspended all executions for the rest of the year, and the head of prisons in the state said over the weekend that he planned to resign.
Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer, whom they had met at a job training camp for troubled teens.
Shipp was 17 years old at the time, meaning that he was spared the death penalty for his part in the attack because he was not yet legally an adult at the time. He remains in prison.
Pike's petition for clemency, denied last week by Republican Governor Bill Lee, argued her death sentence had failed to properly account for Pike's own childhood trauma as the victim of sexual abuse, neglect and untreated mental illness.
In their latest update, Pike's lawyers repeated their call for Lee to use his powers to commute Pike's sentence to the lower punishment of life in prison without parole.
Long the only woman on death row in the state, Pike also has endured nearly 30 years of solitary confinement, her lawyers say.
Dr Joel Zivot, an anaesthesiologist advising Pike's defence team, said on Tuesday that the likelihood of recovering from lethal injection was low.
"Most people who get lethal injection die from it," he told the BBC. "In fact, pretty well everyone, except Christa. So, the fact that she survived it... was unusual."
But there remains a lot of uncertainty and many unknowns, he said, including how much of the pentobarbital got into her system, what her blood levels were after the injection and what her recovery will look like.
"I would not, in any way, say at this point that all the big risks are behind her," he noted.
Zivot had previously said the two doses of pentobarbital she received last week would have been enough that, had it entered her bloodstream in normal circulation, "she would have surely died".
Instead, Zivot said a possible explanation is that instead of entering Pike's bloodstream, the pentobarbital was more likely to have spread across the tissue under her skin.
Pike's lawyers previously warned that her medical history and anatomy — including thrombocytosis (a blood-clotting condition) and small veins — meant there was a risk she would experience "unnecessary" pain and suffering during a lethal injection.
They said on Tuesday that she has endured "severe damage" to her arms.
Pike went from being the first woman Tennessee had tried to put to death since the early 19th century to becoming the first person in the United States known to have survived after execution drugs were administered.

Judge grants emergency order to preserve all evidence in Christa Pike's failed execution
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WZTV) — A Davidson County judge granted a request Wednesday to preserve evidence from Tennessee’s failed attempt to execute Christa Pike, as her attorneys said she is conscious and speaking but facing serious medical complications.
The hearing was held in Davidson County Chancery Court regarding Pike, the woman who survived two lethal injections in an execution attempt last week.
Chancellor I’Ashea Myles said she would issue a written order requiring the state to preserve relevant physical evidence and records from the Sept. 30 execution attempt, including drugs, syringes, IV lines, medical supplies and restraints in its possession.
“This case is unique to say the least,” Chancellor Myles said during the emergency hearing. “In light of the evolving situation, the court will grant the motion to preserve relevant evidence.”
PREVIOUS COVERAGE | Christa Pike awake and speaking after failed execution, lawyers say
The ruling also covers medical waste, drug packaging, photographs, recordings, staff notes, logs and electronic communications including messages about complications, the decision to stop the execution and the call for an ambulance.
This includes possible encrypted communication among TDOC and staff during the timeframe when witnesses say the curtain blinds were closed.
She also directed the Tennessee Department of Correction to try to recover relevant evidence if anything had already been discarded, deleted or destroyed. That instruction did not establish that evidence had been lost.
Ihnen said preserving evidence matters for possible future legal challenges, noting that the state has not promised Pike will never face another execution.
Asked whether the state would reschedule her execution, Ayers said he was not in a position to answer.
Pike’s legal team has renewed its request for Gov. Bill Lee to commute her death sentence to life in prison without parole.
State says evidence is already being preserved
State attorney Will Ayers argued that a separate federal court order already required TDOC to preserve the evidence and that another order was unnecessary.
“TDOC has advised us that evidence, physical evidence, was collected from the execution chamber on the night of September 30th and has been logged into a preservation room,” Ayers told the court.
He said staff collected logbooks, observation logs, medical waste and heart-monitor readouts. He also said TDOC photographed the execution chamber that night.
Ayers cautioned that portions of IV lines may have remained attached to Pike when she was transported to the hospital, putting some potential evidence outside TDOC’s custody.
Pike’s attorney Luke Ihnen said the defense was asking the state to preserve materials it possesses, rather than records or equipment held by the hospital.
“We don’t know what they have because they won’t tell us,” Ihnen said. “And so the preservation order seeks the broadest possible preservation of evidence.”
The ruling concerns saving evidence for litigation. It does not yet require the state to turn that evidence over to Pike’s attorneys or determine what caused the failed execution.
Attorneys describe Pike’s condition
At a news conference after the hearing, attorney Randy Spivey said Pike has pneumonia, a blood clot in her arm and difficulty swallowing that has prevented her from eating. He said she cannot move her arms or hands, which are severely swollen.
“Her hands looked like if you were to blow up a surgical glove,” Spivey said. “It was extraordinary.”
Spivey said the legal team was told Monday that Pike was brain-dead and expected life support to be removed. He said she regained consciousness Tuesday and began speaking.
“I don’t have an explanation for what happened,” Spivey said.
He said Pike was initially confused and disoriented but began remembering details of the execution attempt Wednesday. Her first words upon waking were “Where am I? Who are you?” according to her attorneys.
Spivey said the extent of her recovery remains uncertain.
“We don’t know what function she will regain,” he said.
MORE | Pike’s arms were 'swollen, burned and blistered' after failed execution, attorneys say
Attorney access and restraints discussed
Pike’s attorneys told the court they waited more than two and a half hours to visit her at the hospital Tuesday. Ayers said a visitation process is now in place and denied that TDOC intended to obstruct access to counsel.
Myles said prison officials must respond to attorney visitation requests within two hours. She said Pike should have the same access to counsel she would have in prison, subject to the hospital’s visitation policies.
The judge reserved a decision on whether Pike can use her prison tablet at the hospital, requesting more information from the state about how it works outside a correctional facility.
Attorneys also said one of Pike’s hands and her feet are shackled to her hospital bed. They said medical staff requested removal of the hand restraint because of damage to her arms and hands. The state raised security concerns.
Myles requested documentation from medical personnel before deciding that issue. She also requested the state’s transfer policies before ruling on the attorneys’ request for 48 hours’ notice before Pike is moved from the hospital.
Execution aftermath
After Pike was hospitalized, her attorneys made an emergency court filing Friday alleging that problems with IV access caused the lethal drug to leak into surrounding tissue of her arms. After the injection, her attorneys say that her arms were "swollen, burned and blistered."
A jury convicted Pike in 1996 for the 1995 murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer. Prosecutors say then 18-year-old Pike brutally killed her fellow classmate Slemmer in Knoxville in a jealous rage. Pike, 50, was scheduled on September 30 to become the first woman executed in Tennessee since it was a slave state. She was sentenced to death for the January 1995 murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, a fellow student at the Job Corps center in Knoxville. Pike, then 18, and her 17-year-old boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, lured Slemmer to a secluded area, where she was beaten and killed. Shipp, a juvenile at the time, was sentenced to life in prison.
“She survived two complete rounds of lethal injection per Tennessee’s protocol, despite her attorneys’ warning to the state of specific challenges with her veins,” the attorneys’ statement said.
Those warnings had been explicitly laid out by her attorneys. In their petition for a stay filed with the US Supreme Court, Pike’s lawyers argued that her small, fragile veins and a blood disorder, thrombocytosis, would make establishing IV access difficult and that lethal injection would cause her “serious pain and suffering” in violation of the Eighth Amendment’s ban on cruel and unusual punishment.
On the night of September 30, the execution team took about an hour and multiple attempts to establish IV lines. The first dose of pentobarbital was administered at 7:30 p.m. Central Time. Four minutes later, Pike said, “My arm feels like it’s about to burst open,” according to media witnesses. For the next half hour she breathed deeply, snored, yawned and moved on the gurney. Witnesses described her snoring, grunting and making choking sounds. At 8:05 p.m. the curtains were closed again, and the journalists were left in the dark for some 50 minutes before being ordered out. Pike was then rushed to a Nashville-area hospital.
Her attorneys believe the IV lines were improperly placed or her veins had blown, causing the caustic drug to flow into the tissue of her arms rather than her bloodstream. Her arms were burned, blistered and swollen when she arrived at the hospital. She was placed on a ventilator while doctors worked to clear the pentobarbital from her system, and she remained unconscious through the weekend. After botched execution, US woman was nearly taken off life support before revival
Washington (United States) (AFP) – A convicted US killer who survived a botched execution was almost taken off life support before she regained consciousness, her lawyer said Wednesday, as a court ordered prison authorities to preserve evidence in the case.
Issued on: Modified:
Christa Pike, 50, who was sentenced to death for a murder she committed when she was a teenager, received two supposedly lethal doses of the drug pentobarbital at a Tennessee prison last Wednesday.
She survived the injections, however, and was rushed to a hospital where she was in critical condition for several days, unconscious and on a ventilator.
"On Monday night, it was our understanding that Christa was brain dead, and that life support would be removed the next day," her lawyer Randy Spivey told reporters.
"But on Tuesday, to the shock of everyone... Christa woke up and began talking."
Pike remains shackled to her hospital bed, awake and able to speak a little but incapable of swallowing or moving her arms, according to her attorneys.
"She cannot move either of her arms, both of her arms and hands are tremendously swollen, and we do not know what, if any, function she will regain in her arms," Spivey said, adding that "there's a long road ahead" for her recovery.
"Medical staff have asked that the shackles be removed and have been denied that request," Pike's lawyer Luke Ihnen said at a court hearing.
An anesthesiologist retained by Pike's lawyers as an expert ahead of her execution told the BBC that she was off the ventilator.
She has "no memory, I believe, of the execution attempt," Joel Zivot said, adding that Pike knows her name and thinks it is currently September.
"We have to ask how much suffering is enough? We continue to ask (Tennessee Governor Bill Lee) to commute Christa's death sentence" to life in prison, Spivey said.
The court ordered state corrections officials to preserve all evidence related to the botched execution including medical supplies, waste, and audio and video recordings.
Pike's fate revived debate over capital punishment in the United States.
Lee suspended executions in Tennessee pending an independent investigation and the state's prison chief resigned. Tennessee's correction department has maintained that it followed established protocol.
The state of Texas was scheduled to carry out an execution later Wednesday, the first in the United States since the attempt to put Pike to death.

His lawyers have sought to have his execution postponed, citing Pike's case.

The Death Penalty Information Center, which publishes data and analysis on capital punishment in the United States, said Pike was the first inmate to survive after being injected with lethal doses of execution drugs.
Pike was 18 when she and her boyfriend beat and killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer at a job training camp.

The death penalty has been abolished in 23 of the 50 US states, while three others -- California, Oregon and Pennsylvania -- have moratoriums in place.

Death row inmate Christa Pike is awake and talking after surviving two botched lethal injections, her attorneys said Oct. 6.
The statement was the first public confirmation that the death row inmate has improved since she was taken away in an ambulance from a Nashville prison Sept. 30.
“Despite the severe damage she endured to her arms, she is still handcuffed and shackled to the bed,” her attorneys said, calling her recovery “medically unprecedented.”
Prison officials at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution gave her two doses of pentobarbital after the U.S. Supreme Court lifted a temporary stay of her execution for the 1995 murder of classmate Colleen Slemmer.
The injections didn’t kill her but burned and blistered Pike’s arms, her lawyers said, and she was taken to Vanderbilt University Medical Center hospital where she has received constant care.
“We are incredibly grateful to the first responders and the medical team at the hospital who treated Christa like a human and have provided exceptional care to her,” her attorneys said. “We also want to thank thousands from all over the world who sent messages offering prayers and support for Christa.”
Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee halted executions at the prison pending a review of procedures and protocols following Pike’s incident.
Her lawyers are asking the governor to commute her death sentence to life imprisonment without the possibility of parole.

The Tennessee attorney general and the governor’s office didn’t return requests for comment.

The state requires the placement of two separate intravenous catheters in the prisoner. The pentobarbital is injected into one of the catheters.

Shackled to hospital bed after botched execution, US death row inmate wakes up
Christa Pike has regained consciousness after surviving Tennessee's failed lethal injection attempt. The case now heads to court as her lawyers seek to preserve evidence and challenge the state's conduct.
Christa Pike, the Tennessee death-row inmate who survived an attempt to execute her by lethal injection last week, has regained consciousness and is speaking, her lawyers said on Tuesday.
Pike, 50, remains in hospital under medical care after the failed execution, during which prison officials struggled to establish intravenous lines and administer the lethal drug. Her lawyers said she has suffered severe injuries to both arms and is still “handcuffed and shackled” to her hospital bed.
“Against all odds, Christa Pike is conscious, speaking and continues to receive critical medical care,” her public defence attorneys said in a statement.
Her prognosis remains uncertain, the lawyers said, adding that they expect her recovery to be lengthy. A hearing in Pike’s case is scheduled for Wednesday in Davidson County Chancery Court.
The hearing concerns her lawyers’ request for a court order to preserve evidence from the failed execution. They say the evidence could show that the Tennessee Department of Correction violated Pike’s constitutional rights by subjecting her to cruel and unusual punishment. Pike was not expected to attend the hearing, a spokesperson said.
WHAT HAPPENED DURING THE FAILED EXECUTION
Pike survived Tennessee’s attempt to execute her on the night of September 30 at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville. She has remained hospitalised since then.
She was initially unconscious and critically ill following the procedure. Her lawyers said on Friday that she was on a ventilator while doctors worked to remove pentobarbital, the drug used in the execution attempt, from her system.
The execution lasted roughly 2 hours and descended into a prolonged struggle as Correction Department personnel tried to administer two doses of pentobarbital intravenously, according to Pike’s attorneys and journalists who witnessed the attempt.
Pike was heard gasping, crying, whimpering and breathing heavily during much of the procedure. At one point, she said: “My arm feels like it’s about to burst open.”
Attempts to establish IV lines left both of her arms “swollen, burned and blistered," her lawyers said in court filings. They alleged that pentobarbital, a highly alkaline and caustic substance, leaked into the tissue beneath her skin.
Pike’s lawyers also accused state officials of ignoring warnings from her doctors that her small veins and a blood disorder would make intravenous access particularly difficult.
During the execution attempt, her lawyers filed an emergency motion asking the court to halt the procedure. By that point, prison officials had stopped trying to administer the drugs and called an ambulance, according to court records.
The Tennessee Department of Correction defended its handling of the incident that night, saying it had “followed every step of the state’s lawful, established execution protocol”.
But the episode has since led to changes at the top of the department. Republican Governor Bill Lee announced on Saturday that Correction Department Commissioner Frank Strada had resigned and would leave his post this month.
Lee had already ordered a suspension of all scheduled executions in Tennessee for the remainder of the year and called for an independent review of what happened during Pike’s execution attempt.
PIKE'S CLEMENCY BID CITED CHILDHOOD TRAUMA
Two days before Pike was scheduled to be executed, Lee rejected her request to have her death sentence commuted to life imprisonment without the possibility of parole.
Her clemency petition argued that her death sentence had failed to adequately account for her own history of childhood trauma. Her lawyers said she had been sexually abused, neglected and suffered from untreated mental illness.
Pike had been the only woman on Tennessee’s death row for years and, according to her lawyers, had spent nearly three decades in solitary confinement.
Her case has now put her in a unique position in US capital punishment history. She went from being the first woman Tennessee had attempted to execute in roughly two centuries to becoming the first person in the United States known to have survived after execution drugs were administered.
Death penalty opponents said the incident underscored what they consider the inherent brutality of executions. The failed procedure also renewed questions over whether lethal injections can be carried out without violating constitutional protections against cruel and unusual punishment.
THE 30-YEAR-OLD MURDER CASE
Pike’s death sentence stems from the 1995 torture and killing of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, a schoolmate.
Pike was 18 in January 1995 when she, her 17-year-old boyfriend Tadaryl Shipp and another companion lured Slemmer into a wooded area on the University of Tennessee campus in Knoxville and killed her.
The brutality of the murder attracted widespread media attention. Trial testimony said Shipp carved the shape of a pentagram into Slemmer’s chest, while Pike struck her in the head with a piece of asphalt and later took a fragment of her skull as a souvenir.
Prosecutors said Pike viewed Slemmer as a rival for Shipp’s affections.
Pike and Shipp confessed to the killing and were convicted of first-degree murder. Pike was sentenced to death, while Shipp received life in prison with the possibility of parole.
Their co-defendant, Shadolla Peterson, who was 18 at the time and acted as a lookout, testified for the prosecution and received probation.

The account of her current condition comes entirely from statements made by her attorneys and relayed by the accounts and outlets named above. What is known is that Pike was scheduled for execution and that the process did not proceed as planned. She was taken to a hospital and placed on a ventilator, a fact reported across multiple outlets. Her attorney initially described her as critically ill and unconscious. The update Tuesday -- that she is now awake and speaking -- came from the same legal team.
The reaction has spread across national news accounts and capital punishment observers, with each new outlet attributing the condition update to Pike's lawyers. No hospital statement, no independent medical record, and no official correction from the Tennessee Department of Correction has been produced to corroborate the attorneys' account. Here is what the establishment media will not say plainly: a woman sentenced to death survived the state's attempt to kill her, and now her lawyers are the only source for what happens next. This week, she said Tennessee authorities need to “make this right” and make sure that Pike remains on death row.
Pike, 50, would have been the first woman executed in Tennessee in 200 years.
Gov. Bill Lee ordered an independent review of the failed execution last week and paused all executions for the rest of the year. Pike’s attorneys have said they believe problems with the IV lines may have caused the pentobarbital to flow into her body instead of her bloodstream.
On Saturday, Lee announced the resignation of Frank Strada, the state’s top prison official.
In a statement, Strada said he believed the state Department of Correction had carried out its responsibilities “in accordance with the established protocol.” But stepping aside, he added, was in the “best interest of Tennesseans as the independent review moves forward.”
Slemmer’s mother said that after what she has been through with the failed execution attempt, Tennessee authorities including the governor “owe me big time.”
