sources.news_title: Christa Pike Conscious And Speaking After Surviving Failed Execution Attempt, Attorneys Say
sources.text:
Christa Pike is conscious and speaking nearly a week after Tennessee’s attempt to execute her by lethal injection failed, according to her attorneys, marking a significant improvement after she was hospitalized in critical condition.
Pike, 50, remains hospitalized and is receiving critical medical care following the Sept. 30 execution attempt. Her attorneys said Tuesday that while she has regained consciousness, the extent of her recovery remains uncertain.
“Her recovery is medically unprecedented,” her attorneys said, adding that they expect her recovery to be lengthy.
The update comes days after Pike was reported to be unconscious and on a ventilator following the execution attempt. Her lawyers say she suffered severe injuries to both arms during the procedure.
What happened during the execution attempt
Pike was scheduled to die by lethal injection at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville on Sept. 30.
According to court filings from her attorneys, execution personnel had difficulty establishing intravenous access before administering two doses of pentobarbital, the drug Tennessee uses for lethal injections.
Pike’s attorneys allege that at least seven needles were used in attempts to establish IV access. Their filing says Pike could be heard crying and breathing loudly during portions of the procedure and at one point complained that her arm felt as though it was going to burst.
When Pike arrived at a Nashville-area hospital, her attorneys said both of her arms were swollen, burned and blistered. They contend the injuries resulted from problems administering the lethal-injection drug.
The Tennessee Department of Correction has maintained that officials followed the state’s established execution protocol. In a statement issued the night of the attempted execution, the department said the protocol had been followed and that it did not permit additional procedures beyond those already performed. Pike was subsequently transported to an outside medical facility.
The department confirmed Tuesday that Pike remains hospitalized but said federal medical privacy laws prevent it from providing or confirming details about her condition.
Pike remains restrained in hospital, lawyers say
Pike’s attorneys said Tuesday that she remains handcuffed and shackled to her hospital bed despite the injuries to her arms.
They also thanked first responders and the medical team caring for Pike and renewed their call for Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee to commute her death sentence to life in prison without the possibility of parole.
Her attorneys have separately gone to court seeking to ensure that physical, written and electronic evidence connected to the execution attempt is preserved. A status conference in that case is scheduled for Wednesday.
Tennessee halts executions
The failed execution has prompted a broader examination of Tennessee’s death penalty system.
Lee ordered a comprehensive third-party review of what happened and halted the state’s remaining execution scheduled for 2026. The governor said carrying out a death sentence is one of the state’s most serious responsibilities and that Tennesseans expect the process to be legal, constitutional and effective.
The incident comes after Tennessee experienced another troubled execution attempt earlier this year. In May, officials were unable to execute Tony Carruthers after encountering problems establishing required IV access.
Pike was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer.
Pike was 18 at the time of the killing. She was convicted of participating in Slemmer’s torture and murder near the University of Tennessee’s agricultural campus in Knoxville and has spent decades on death row.
Her execution would have made her the first woman put to death by Tennessee in roughly two centuries.
Pike’s attorneys had raised concerns before the execution about whether lethal injection could be carried out safely in her case, citing medical conditions and difficulties involving her veins. Those concerns have taken on new significance following the failed procedure.
What happens next remains uncertain.
